water_regime — removed on audit: Verified live against all four cited pages. The record sets water_regime='keep_moist' citing only MOBOT's boilerplate prose 'Easily grown in moist, average, well-drained soils' — but MOBOT's own structured fields on that SAME page say 'Water: Medium' and 'Tolerate: Drought', which the record never cites. This isn't an isolated omission: every single admissible source used elsewhere in this record independently rates the species as drought-tolerant via a dedicated structured field, not just incidental prose — NC State: tags '#drought tolerant', 'Particularly Resistant To...: Heat, drought, poor soil', 'Resistance To Challenges: Drought Heat Poor Soil', 'Landscape Theme: Drought Tolerant Garden' (and its own Issues line warns 'subject to root rot if kept too moist' — the record used this exact quote for the fertilizer field but never let it inform water_regime); UF/IFAS: dedicated field 'Drought tolerance: moderate'; RHS: dedicated field 'Drought Resistance: Yes' (confirmed via full page text, alongside 'Moisture: Moist but well-drained'). This is precisely the structural-check-1 scenario: genuinely opposing signals on a harm-capable field (moist-soil prose vs. four independent drought-tolerance ratings, plus an explicit root-rot-from-overwatering warning) were resolved by picking one value instead of reflecting the conflict or leaving it null. 'keep_moist' risks steering a caregiver toward overwatering a plant every source calls at least moderately drought-tolerant, with NC State explicitly warning that overwatering causes root rot in this species.

is_houseplant — removed on audit: false is asserted with ZERO citation entry in the citations array — no quote anywhere backs this field. The record's own 'unknowns' text admits 'no admissible source describes Amaranthus tricolor being grown indoors long-term as a houseplant' and then converts that silence into a stated 'false' rather than null, which is exactly the negative-claim-dressed-as-absence-of-evidence pattern the audit brief calls out (is_houseplant=false 'cited to a source that only discussed seed-starting logistics' / an unaddressed field should be null). I fetched all four source pages directly: none of NC State, MOBOT, UF/IFAS, or RHS discusses indoor/houseplant cultivation in either direction. If anything cuts against the blanket claim, it's RHS's cultivation note that the plant 'can be grown under glass in full light in a peat-free, loam-based potting compost' (protected/greenhouse pot culture) — not proof of houseplant use, but it shows the sources don't actually foreclose indoor-adjacent cultivation either. This field should be null, not false.

records.water_estimate_basis: Estimate, not a stated interval. Derived from University of Maryland Extension's field cut-flower production guidance that transplanted Celosia should receive about one inch of water per week from irrigation or rainfall (the source's "each week" was converted to a 7-day interval). This assumes outdoor garden-bed/field growing conditions during active growth, not container or indoor culture, and UMD frames it as a minimum to prevent moisture-stress stunting rather than a fixed schedule.
unknowns: chill_damage_f: no admissible source states a frost/cold damage-onset temperature. NC State only tags the species 'frost tender' with no number; UMD gives growth-effect thresholds (below 60°F stunts plants and causes premature flowering; below 50°F reduces flowering vigor) which describe growth performance, not tissue damage onset; RHS's H2 hardiness rating ("tolerant of low temperatures, but not surviving being frozen (1 to 5)" °C) is explicitly a survival/tolerance floor for the plant, which the task instructions say must not be mapped onto chill_damage_f.

day_f_min/max and night_f_min/max: the only day-vs-night-specific temperatures found (UMD: germinate seed at 65-70°F at night, 80-85°F during the day) describe seed-germination conditions specifically, not an ongoing growing-temperature range for an established plant, so they were not mapped onto these fields to avoid presenting germination-stage data as general care advice.

humidity_need: evidence is stage- and context-dependent rather than a single average. NC State tags the species 'humidity tolerant' and says it 'thrives in heat and humidity'; UMD's greenhouse production notes say vegetative growth 'benefits from high humidity' but that plants nearing harvest want 'shade and less humidity' for postharvest quality. No single value applies across life stages/settings.

fertilize_interval_days: UMD (greenhouse cut-flower production) states 'weekly applications of a dilute complete fertilizer,' while RHS (general outdoor/container cultivation) states 'Apply a balanced liquid fertiliser every two weeks.' These are different growing contexts giving different numbers for the same measure (7 vs 14 days), so no single value was taken rather than picking one context over the other.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good: UMD gives '3,500 to 5,000-foot candles of light' specifically for vegetative growth in commercial greenhouse cut-flower production, not for general indoor/houseplant window or grow-light conditions, so it was not used for these fields despite is_houseplant being true.

soil_base: sources describe both container/potting use (RHS: 'Grow in peat-free, loam-based potting compost') and open garden-bed use (RHS 'Outdoors, plant in... fertile soil'; NC State soil-texture tags for in-ground planting), with no source stating a single standardized soil-mix category, so no soil_base enum value was assigned.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: set from NC State's general tag 'Soil pH: Neutral (6.0-8.0)'. UMD separately states cut-flower field production 'thrives in well-drained soil with a pH of 6.0 to 6.4' -- a narrower, production-specific optimum nested inside NC State's broader tolerance range rather than a contradiction, but noted here since a different number appears in another admissible source.

water_regime: no source uses language matching any of the enum categories (keep_moist / dry_surface_between / dry_thoroughly_between / keep_barely_moist). Available quotes describe drought/dry-soil tolerance, an 'occasionally dry' soil-drainage tag, and a weekly irrigation amount for field production -- none map cleanly onto one regime category, so it was left null rather than inferred.

humidity_pct_min/max, direct_sun_hours_max, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength, water_dormant_days_est, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, cool_rest_note: no admissible source gave a quotable value for these fields.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: Value 'fast' is not literally supported by either cited quote. NC State's page (verified by direct fetch) tags the species 'Good Drainage' and 'Occasionally Dry' -- not 'fast'. The RHS citation, explicitly invoked to 'support soil_drainage fast', quotes 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained', which is a moisture-retention descriptor and arguably cuts against a 'fast'-drainage characterization rather than supporting it. 'Fast' is an inferential leap from tag-based drainage/moisture descriptors, not a value stated by either admissible source.

toxic_to_pets: no admissible source addresses toxicity to cats, dogs, or other pets for Coleus; NC State documents toxicity to humans only (skin irritation/contact dermatitis from leaf contact).

water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_check_depth_cm, water_estimate_basis, cool_rest_note: no admissible source gives a calendar-based watering interval, a checking depth in centimeters, or dormancy/rest information; Clemson's actionable guidance is condition-based ('water when the entire top inch of soil is dry') rather than a day count, and converting 'top inch' to a centimeter figure not stated in the source was avoided.

fertilize_interval_days — removed on audit: The value 14 is not literally present in its own cited quote. The RHS quote says 'apply a high-nitrogen every 2 weeks' — the source states '2' (weeks), never '14' (days); 14 is a silent unit conversion the researcher performed, not a number stated in the quote, which fails the re-derivation check. Independently verified against the live RHS page: the cultivation text is 'Under glass grow in peat-free potting compost in full light or partial shade. Water freely in growth and apply a high-nitrogen every 2 weeks' — an indoor/greenhouse ('under glass') fertilizing cadence with no month restriction. This is then paired in the record with fertilize_active_months (6,7,8), which comes from a *different* source (Clemson) describing a *different* context — outdoor garden-bed fertilizing restricted to a mid-summer boost with specific NPK formulations (24-8-16 or 17-4-17), no stated interval. Neither source actually supports 'fertilize every 14 days, active only in June–August' as a combined regimen; that composite claim is synthesized across two sources describing different growing contexts (greenhouse vs. outdoor bed) and time scopes (year-round growth vs. summer-only), which is a genuine over-reach on a field that governs a real feeding schedule.

is_houseplant — removed on audit: Value is false, cited to NC State's quote 'Use these plants to add summer color to the border of cottage, cutting and butterfly gardens.' That sentence only describes typical outdoor garden placement -- it never addresses whether the mature plant can or cannot be grown indoors. This is exactly the trap the audit brief warns about: an unaddressed question (indoor growability) dressed up as a stated negative fact. The field should be null, not false.

water_regime — removed on audit: Set to 'dry_thoroughly_between' on the UGA CAES quote 'water sparingly but when you do, water deeply, training those roots to go deep.' But the record's own Missouri Botanical Garden citation for the same plant says 'Appreciates even moisture, but tolerates some dry soils' -- i.e. the plant is described as preferring consistent moisture, not an infrequent deep-dry-down cycle. That is a genuine cross-source tension on the same harm-capable field (an owner following 'dry thoroughly between' waterings would be under-watering a plant MOBOT says appreciates even moisture). Additionally, the UGA piece is a journalistic 'Field Report' about roadside plantings ('Old-fashioned cosmos are breathtaking along Georgia highways') and the pasted quote never ties the advice specifically to Cosmos bipinnatus as opposed to cosmos plantings/genus generally. Given the unresolved conflict, this should be null rather than a picked value.

The quote supports that Bidens formosa is listed as a synonym, but it does not itself substantiate the specific 'name status: Correct' assertion built on top of it.

is_houseplant — removed on audit: Set to false with no supporting citation at all -- there is no citations[] entry whose claim addresses is_houseplant, only a rationale buried in 'unknowns.' The stated rationale is that no admissible source describes indoor/houseplant cultivation and every source (RHS, MOBOT, NC State) discusses only outdoor bedding/border/rock-garden/lawn use. That is absence of evidence, not evidence of absence: none of the three sources make an affirmative claim that Bellis perennis is unsuited to or not grown as an indoor plant. This is exactly the anti-pattern the audit brief calls out -- a negative asserted as fact when the sources simply never addressed the question. Per instruction, an unaddressed field should be left null, not stated as false.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: Value 'moderate' is not what either citation's quote says. MOBOT's quote reads '...consistently moist, well-drained soils...' and RHS's quote reads 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained' -- both are explicit, standard horticultural 'well-drained' classifications (RHS's own controlled-vocabulary soil-moisture field), not 'moderate' drainage. Neither quote uses or implies the word 'moderate,' and well-drained is normally its own distinct category from moderate/average drainage. The record silently reclassified 'well-drained' into 'moderate' without any source stating that value, which fails the 'does the quote ACTUALLY state this value' check.

normalizations: 2026-08-21: landed with zero manual fixes. The audit caught a subtler variant of the b10 conflict-resolution failure than has shown up before: Joseph's Coat's water_regime was set to keep_moist citing one source's soft prose ('moist, well-drained soils'), while that same source's own structured fields ('Water: Medium', 'Tolerate: Drought') and three other independently-cited sources' dedicated drought-tolerance ratings all pointed the other way -- plus an explicit root-rot-from-overwatering warning the record had already quoted for a different field without letting it inform this one. Correctly recognized as the same structural conflict the rule exists for and nulled, even though the disagreement here was prose-vs-structured-data within and across sources rather than a flat boolean contradiction. Coleus resolved to Coleus scutellarioides (given as Plectranthus scutellarioides), backed independently by NC State and RHS on the same genus reclassification.
